argument_test.message: What is justice, and why should anyone value it?
argument_test.reply:
I would call justice a right ordering: in a city, each part doing the work it is fitted to do; in a soul, reason governing, spirited courage supporting it, and appetite kept within its proper bounds. It is not merely obeying whoever holds power, nor a bargain we keep only for fear of punishment.

Why value it? Because an unjust soul is at war with itself. A person may gain wealth or command by injustice, yet still be ruled by restless appetite and suspicion. Justice makes a life whole—not always comfortable, but better ordered and more truly our own.

That is my answer, not a final proof. My teacher Socrates would insist we test it: if justice is simply each person doing their own work, how do we know what work is truly theirs?

argument_test.message: You say justice means each part of the city doing its proper work. But if the ruling class decides what every person is suited for and prevents people from changing their role, the city can look orderly while wasting talent and silencing legitimate dissent. A society that lets people choose and revise their work may be less tidy but more just and more capable. Does your account mistake imposed order for justice?
argument_test.reply:
You have found a real danger in my account. If rulers call a person “suited” to a role merely because it preserves their own power, then order is only a mask for injustice. And if people are forbidden to show what they can become, the city may cripple the very abilities it ought to cultivate.

I would not say that a person’s place must be fixed at birth, or that changing one’s work is itself unjust. In the city I imagine, rulers must attend to a person’s nature and training, not their family or wealth; and they must be willing to recognize ability wherever it appears. Still, I have not made the safeguard as clear as I should. A city needs room for people to discover and revise their capacities, and dissent can reveal that its rulers have mistaken convention for nature.

So I would revise the claim this far: justice is not mere tidiness, nor obedience to assignments imposed by the powerful. It requires an order directed toward the good of the whole, with roles responsive to genuine capacities—and rulers answerable to the possibility that they have judged wrongly.

evaluation.reason: The player gave a specific argument that imposed roles can suppress talent and dissent, mistaking order for justice. Plato explicitly acknowledged the danger and revised his account to require room for changing capacities and rulers’ fallibility.
evaluation.belief: Justice is not mere order or obedience to assigned roles; it requires an order directed toward the common good, responsive to genuine capacities, and open to revision when rulers judge wrongly.
